title: Unit 1b Title: Expressions
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 1b, which covers C++ expressions, variable review, assignment, casting, and math library functions.
main_text: Unit 1b - Expressions. Instructor: Mark Redekopp.

title: Scalar Processing Programs (Recap)
summary: Recaps the (Prompt)-Input-Process-Output (P)IPO pattern from the previous unit as a lead-in to a deeper look at variables and expressions.
main_text: Scalar Processing Programs. A real program needs to get input values and produce output (text to the screen). These scalar processing programs generally follow a simple sequence: (Prompt)-Input-Process-Output (P)IPO. 1. Prompt the user for 1 or more (some constant amount of) input values. 2. Receive the input value(s). 3. Using the input, perform operations (processing) to produce 1 or more (some constant amount of) desired output values. 4. Display the output value(s). Note: A scalar (in this context) refers to 1, 2, or some small constant number of input values (as opposed to a variable number of input values).
notes_text: This is a recap of the same slide from Unit 1a, reused here to re-establish the (P)IPO pattern before diving into expressions, variables, and assignment in this unit.

images.description: Three annotated terminal transcripts illustrating the Prompt-Input-Process-Output pattern: an egg-to-dozens converter, a tuition cost calculator, and a rectangle/triangle area calculator, each with prompt (1), input (2), and output (4) steps labeled, and the caption 'Where is the processing?'
labels: How many eggs do you have?

title: Section Divider: Review of Variables - Dos and Don'ts
summary: Section header slide introducing a review of key variable rules (dos and don'ts) before moving into assignment and expressions.
main_text: REVIEW OF VARIABLES. Dos and Don'ts
notes_text: Precedes three 'Fact' slides covering variable storage, declaration requirements, and initialization requirements.

title: Fact 1: Variables Store Data
summary: States that a variable is a memory storage location used to store data until it is used or updated, illustrated with a simple int example and a 'storage bin' analogy.
main_text: Fact 1: Variables Store Data. A variable is a memory storage location to store data until you want to use or update it.
notes_text: The code declares 'int y = 2;', prints 'y*4' (8, though not explicitly shown as output), then reassigns 'y = 3;'. The storage-bin graphic shows the bin labeled 'y' holding the value 2, with an arrow depicting the value 3 being poured in to replace it.

images.description: A graphic of a storage bin labeled 'y' holding the value 2, with a red arrow pouring in the new value 3 from above, illustrating a variable as a labeled container whose contents can be overwritten.

title: Fact 2: Variables Must Be Declared Before Use
summary: States that variables must be declared before use, giving the declaration syntax and contrasting a 'bad' example (using undeclared variables) with a 'good' example (each variable declared exactly once before use).
main_text: Fact 2: Variable Must Be Declared. Variables must be declared before they can be used. Format: type name [ = initial_value]; (e.g. char a = '!';)
notes_text: The 'Bad' code panel assigns 'v = 2;' and uses 'x + v' without ever declaring either variable (both would cause compile errors, annotated 'v assigned but not declared' and 'x is used but not declared'). The 'Good' panel fixes both by declaring 'int v = 2;' and 'int x = -1;' before use.

images.description: Two side-by-side red/green code panels: the red 'Bad' panel shows a variable 'v' being assigned without declaration and a variable 'x' being used without declaration; the green 'Good' panel shows both properly declared with types ('int v = 2;' and 'int x = -1;') before being used, illustrating the requirement that every variable be declared exactly once before use.
labels: x is used but not declared
Good! (Each variable must be declared exactly once.)

title: Fact 3: Uninitialized Variables Hold Garbage Values
summary: Warns that an uninitialized variable can hold a random, garbage value and must not be used before being initialized via cin or the '=' operator, shown with contrasting bad/good code examples.
main_text: Fact 3: Uninitialized Variables = Garbage. An uninitialized variable CAN have a RANDOM, GARBAGE value! Do NOT use a variable before you initialize it! Can use cin or `=` to initialize.
notes_text: The 'Bad' panel declares 'int v;' and immediately prints it with cout before ever assigning it a value (illustrated with a trash-can icon), while the 'Good' panel declares 'int v;' then uses 'cin >> v;' to initialize it via keyboard input before printing.

images.description: Two side-by-side red/green code panels illustrating uninitialized variable use: the red 'Bad' panel declares 'int v;' and immediately prints it with cout (accompanied by a trash-can icon symbolizing garbage data) before any value is assigned; the green 'Good' panel declares 'int v;' then reads a value into it with 'cin >> v;' before printing, ensuring it holds a defined value.

title: C++ Types, Storage, and Range
summary: Presents a reference table of core C++ data types -- int/unsigned int, char, float/double, string/char[], and bool -- with their storage size in bytes/bits and value ranges, alongside an annotated declaration example for each.
main_text: C++ Types, Storage, and Range. int / unsigned int: Integer values, 4 bytes/32 bits, range -2 billion to +2 billion (int) or 0 to +4 billion (unsigned int). char: Text character or small integral value, 1 byte/8 bits, ASCII characters / -128 to +127. float / double: Rational/real values, float is 4 bytes/32 bits with 7 significant digits * 10^+/-308, double is 8 bytes/64 bits with 16 significant digits * 10^+/-308. string / char[]: Arbitrary text, arbitrary size / 1 byte per char. bool: True/False value, 1 byte/8 bits, true / false.
notes_text: The accompanying code declares one variable of each type: 'int a = -1;', 'unsigned int b = 2;', 'char c = 'A';' (annotated 'A'=65), 'float d1 = 1.5;', 'double d2 = 3.14;', 'char e[6] = "Hello";', 'string f = "Goodbye";', and 'bool g = true;', with '#include <string>' required for the string type. Small callouts distinguish which parts of the syntax are 'Constant' vs. 'Variable'.

title: When To Introduce a Variable
summary: Explains three reasons to introduce a variable: to hold input or run-time-changing values, to store a value computed now for reuse later, and to make code more readable, contrasted with a single unreadable expression.
main_text: When To Introduce a Variable. When a value will be input (via cin) and/or change at run-time (as the program executes). When a value is computed/updated now but needs to be used (potentially many times) later. To make the code more readable by another human.
notes_text: The username/password blank ('______ username, password;' with 'cin >> username >> password;') is left incomplete on this early version of the slide, to be filled in with the type 'string' -- this is later completed on the solutions slide near the end of the deck (slide 33). The readability example contrasts a single dense expression 'double a = (x+34) * (n*6.25);' with the same computation broken into named intermediate variables 'height', 'width', and 'area'.

images.description: A screenshot of a login form (username 'redekopp' and a masked password field with a 'Sign in' button) representing a scenario where input variables are needed, paired with a screenshot of a spreadsheet with a column of numbers and a 'SUM' row representing a scenario where a computed running total needs to be stored and reused.
labels: Welcome. Please sign in to continue.

title: What Variables Might Be Needed: Video Playback (Discussion Prompt)
summary: An interactive discussion prompt asking students to brainstorm what variables a video playback application (like YouTube) might need, shown with empty storage-bin placeholders to be filled in during class.
main_text: What Variables Might Be Needed. Video playback (e.g. YouTube)
notes_text: This is a fill-in-the-blank/discussion slide: three empty storage-bin icons are shown without labels, intended to be filled in live during lecture with variable names/types (e.g. url, volume, fullscreen flag). The completed version of this exercise appears later in the deck (slide 34) with the answers 'string url', 'int volume', and 'bool fullScreen'.

images.description: Three empty gray storage-bin icons arranged side by side with no labels, used as placeholders for students to brainstorm and fill in variable names/types needed for a video playback application during class discussion.

title: C/C++ Variable Names: Rules and Naming Conventions
summary: Covers the syntax rules for legal C/C++ variable names (allowed starting/subsequent characters), advises using descriptive names over cryptic ones, and explains camelCase and snake_case naming conventions for multi-word names.
main_text: C/C++ Variable Names. Must start with: A-Z, a-z, _. Then contain any alphanumeric character: 0-9, A-Z, a-z, _. But no punctuation or spaces other than underscores. Avoid cryptic names (myvar1, a_thing). Use descriptive names: numStudents vs. n, done_flag vs. d, appt2_time vs. a2t. What's in a name? For multi-word variable names, most programmers use either camel-case or snake-case to write compound names. Camel case: Capitalize the first letter of each word (with the possible exception of the first word), e.g. myVariable, isHighEnough. Snake case: Separate each word with an underscore '_', e.g. my_variable, is_high_enough.
notes_text: Emphasizes readability and maintainability of code through good naming practice, distinct from the strict legal syntax rules for what characters are allowed in an identifier.

title: Section Divider: Variable Assignment Using the '=' Operator
summary: Section header slide introducing the assignment operator topic, transitioning from variable naming rules into how assignment actually works.
main_text: VARIABLE ASSIGNMENT USING '=' OPERATOR
notes_text: Marks the start of the assignment-operator-focused portion of the unit, including right-to-left evaluation order, shortcut operators, and increment/decrement operators.

title: Variable Assignment Sequence: Decode the Rule
summary: A warm-up puzzle slide asking students to decode a reversed phrase to discover the key rule of how assignment works in C++.
main_text: Variable Assignment Sequence. Decode the text below for understanding the key rule of how assignment works: "tfel ot thgir krow"
notes_text: The reversed text "tfel ot thgir krow" decodes (reading each word backwards) to "work right to left", previewing the core rule taught on the next slide: assignment expressions are evaluated on the right-hand side first, then the result is stored into the variable on the left-hand side.

title: Assignment Operator (=): Right-to-Left Evaluation
summary: Explains that the assignment operator updates a variable's value and always works right to left: the right-hand expression is evaluated using current variable values before the left-hand variable is updated with the new result.
main_text: Assignment operator (=). Assignment operator ('=') updates a variable's value. Assignment works right to left. Evaluate the expression on the right using the current values of the variables before updating the variable on the left with a new value.
notes_text: Worked example: 'int x = 1;' followed by 'x = x + 3;'. The diagram shows the CPU first reading the current value of x (1) from its storage bin, computing 1 + 3 = 4, and only then overwriting the bin labeled x with the new value 4 -- visually reinforcing the right-to-left order of operations.

images.description: A two-step diagram illustrating right-to-left assignment evaluation for 'x = x + 3;': first, the current value of x (1) flows from its storage bin into the CPU; the CPU computes 1 + 3 = 4; then the new value 4 flows back and overwrites the storage bin labeled x.

title: Assignment Operator (=) Summary
summary: Summarizes assignment operator syntax and semantics: 'variable = expression;' means store the computed right-hand-side result into the left-hand-side variable's memory location, distinct from the equality operator '=='.
main_text: Assignment operator (=) Summary. Syntax: variable = expression; Should be read: Store the resulting value of <expression> into memory location of <variable>. Example: z = x + y - (2*z); (LHS) (RHS). LHS = Left Hand-Side, RHS = Right Hand Side. Key to understanding assignment: (i.e. work right to left). If variable appears on both sides, we use the old/current value of the variable on the RHS. = does NOT mean "compare for equality"; that is the == operator.
notes_text: The three numbered steps shown are: 1) Compute Expression Result (evaluate the RHS), 2) Store (the computed value), 3) Var. (into the LHS variable's memory) -- formalizing the right-to-left process introduced on the previous slide.

title: Common Mistake: Forgetting to Assign
summary: Warns that computing an expression without assigning it to a variable discards the result, contrasting 'x + 1;' (which computes and throws away the result) with 'x = x + 1;' (which actually updates x).
main_text: Common Mistake: Forgetting to Assign. Without assignment, computed values are lost! int x = 0; x + 1; // Takes x's value and adds 1 but DOES NOT update x (just throws the result away). x = x + 1; // Using assignment, x actually updates.
notes_text: Two before/after diagrams contrast the outcomes: writing 'x + 1' computes 0+1=1 in the CPU but the result is discarded (illustrated with a trash can) and x remains 0 afterward; writing 'x = x + 1' computes the same result but stores it back into x, which becomes 1 afterward.

images.description: Two side-by-side before/after diagrams: the left ('x + 1;') shows the CPU computing 0+1 but the result being thrown into a trash can, leaving x unchanged at 0 afterward, marked with a red X; the right ('x = x + 1;') shows the CPU computing 0+1 and the result 1 being stored back into x's bin, marked with a green checkmark.

title: Shortcut Assignment Statements (Compound Assignment Operators)
summary: Introduces compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=, etc.) as shorthand for 'var = var op expr;', with a worked code example tracing the resulting values of x and y.
main_text: Shortcut Assignment Statements. A common task is to update a variable by adding, subtracting, multiplying, etc. some value to it: x = x + 4; y = y * 2.5; C/C++ provide a shortcut for writing these statements: x += 4; y *= 2.5; The substitution is: var op= expr; Becomes var = var op expr; Shorthand operators exist for most operators: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, &=, ...
notes_text: The code example traces 'int x = 1; double y = 3.75;' through 'x += 5;' (x becomes 6), 'y -= 2.25;' (y becomes 1.5), 'x /= 3;' (x becomes 2), and 'y *= 2.0' (y becomes 3.0), demonstrating each compound operator's effect step by step.

title: Post-Increment/Decrement Operators (++/--)
summary: Introduces the ++ and -- operators as shortcuts for adding or subtracting 1 from a variable, equivalent to x += 1 and x -= 1, with a brief mention that pre-increment/decrement nuances will be covered in a future lecture.
main_text: Post-Increment/Decrement. Adding 1 to a variable (e.g. x += 1) and subtracting 1 from a variable (e.g. x -= 1) are extremely common operations (especially when we cover loops). The ++ and -- operators offer a shortcut to "increment-by-1" or "decrement-by-1": performs (x += 1) or (x -= 1). x++; // If x was 2 it will be updated to 3 (x = x + 1). x--; // If x was 2 it will be updated to 1 (x = x - 1). Note: There are some nuances to this operator and an alternative known as PRE-increment/decrement that we will discuss in future lectures, but this is sufficient for now.
notes_text: Explicitly foreshadows a future lecture on the distinction between pre- and post-increment/decrement, indicating this slide covers only the simplified post-increment/decrement behavior for now.

title: Exercise: Trace the Code (Variable Tracing Practice)
summary: A code-tracing exercise asking students to track the values of 'value' and 'amount' line by line through a program involving assignment, integer/double division, and modulus, using a table template.
main_text: Exercise: Trace the Code Below. Trace the code below. Make a table of the variables and track their value at each line of code. Program: int value = 1; value = (value + 5) * (value - 3); cout << value << endl; double amount = 2.5; value = 7; amount = value + 6 / amount; cout << amount << endl; cout << value % 3 << endl;
notes_text: A small example (int x = 0; x = x + 3;) illustrates the tracing table format, distinguishing 'current-value of x (0)' from 'new-value of x (3)' as column headers for the trace table. The solved answers for this exercise appear later in the deck (slide 35): value prints -12, then amount prints 9.4 (using double division since amount is a double), and value % 3 prints 1.

title: More Exercises: Predict the Output
summary: Two 'predict the output' practice programs: one testing modulus/division/precedence with mixed int/double types, and one computing dozens-to-items conversion alongside a GPA calculation with a hint about integer vs. double division.
main_text: More Exercises. What is printed by the following two programs? Program 1: int x = 5; int y = 3; double z = x % y * 6 + x / y; cout << z << endl; z = 1.0 / 4 * (z - x) + y; cout << z << endl; Program 2: int dozens = 3; double gpa = 2.0; int num = 12 * dozens; gpa = (2 * 4.0) + (4 * 3.7); // gpa updated to 22.8; gpa /= 6; // gpa = gpa / 6 ... integer or double division?; cout << dozens << " dozen is " << num << " items." << endl; cout << "Your gpa is " << gpa << endl;
notes_text: Program 2's inline comment poses a rhetorical question about whether 'gpa /= 6' performs integer or double division -- since gpa is already a double, the division is a double (floating-point) division. The solved outputs for both programs appear later in the deck (slide 36): Program 1 prints 13 then 5; Program 2 prints '3 dozen is 36 items.' then 'Your gpa is 3.8333'.

title: [Optional] Tracing Practice with Solution
summary: An optional worked example showing that variables can be reassigned as often as desired using '=', with a full program tracing an int and a char through two rounds of assignment and its printed output.
main_text: [Optional] Tracing Practice with Solution. We can use `=` to update a variable as often as we like. Program: int w=0; char x='z'; // variables don't have to be initialized when declared; w = 300; x = 'a'; cout << w << " " << x << endl; w = -75; x = '!'; cout << w << " " << x << endl;
notes_text: This slide includes its own answer directly (unlike other exercises whose solutions appear later): the program's console output is shown as '300 a' followed by '-75 !', reinforcing that assignment is one of the most common operations in programs and that declared variables need not be initialized at the point of declaration.

title: Section Divider: Casting and Using Math Library Functions
summary: Section header slide transitioning from assignment topics into type casting and calling built-in math/library functions.
main_text: CASTING AND USING MATH LIBRARY FUNCTIONS
notes_text: Marks the start of the casting- and library-function-focused portion of the unit.

title: Casting Motivation: Fixing Integer Division
summary: Motivates type casting by showing how integer division causes unexpected results (e.g. 5 + 3/2), and demonstrates implicit casting with constants versus explicit C-style and C++-style casting when variables are involved, with a caution about a common casting mistake.
main_text: Casting Motivation. Def. casting: Temporarily converting the type of a data value. What is the result of 5 + 3/2? To achieve the correct answer we could: Use implicit casting (mixed expression) -- could just write 5 + 3.0 / 2; if an operator is applied to mixed type inputs, the less expressive type is automatically and implicitly cast (promoted) to the more expressive type (int is promoted to double). But what if instead of constants we have variables? int x=5, y=3, z=2; x + y/z; // Won't work & you can't write y.0. We can perform an explicit cast using either the C or C++ syntax: x + (double) y / z; // C style casting method; x + static_cast<double>(y) / z; // C++ style casting method. BE CAREFUL!! This won't yield the 6.5 answer you expect: x + static_cast<double>(y/z); // Why not?
notes_text: The final caution example ('x + static_cast<double>(y/z);') is a deliberate trap: because the division 'y/z' still happens as integer division before the cast is applied, casting the already-truncated integer result to double does not recover the fractional part -- illustrating that operator precedence/grouping matters when placing a cast.

title: Math & Other Library Functions
summary: Lists several commonly used predefined C++ functions (sqrt, pow, sin/cos/tan, abs, max/min), which headers they come from, and how to call them within expressions or assignments.
main_text: Math & Other Library Functions. C++ predefines a variety of functions for you. Here are a few of them: sqrt(x): returns the square root of x (in <cmath>). pow(x, y): returns x to the power y (in <cmath>). sin(x)/cos(x)/tan(x): returns the sine/cosine/tangent of x if x is in radians (in <cmath>). abs(x): returns the absolute value of x (in <cstdlib>). max(x, y) and min(x, y): returns the maximum/minimum of x and y (in <algorithm>). You call these by writing them similarly to how you would use a function in mathematics, using parentheses for the inputs (aka arguments). Result is replaced into bigger expression. Must #include the correct library; #includes tell the compiler about the various pre-defined functions that your program may choose to call.
notes_text: The example code calls 'cos(0)' directly in an assignment (res = 1.0), calls 'sqrt(2) / 2' as part of a larger expression, and calls 'max(34, 56)' directly inside a cout statement (outputs 56), with a reference link to http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/ for the full cmath function reference.

title: #include Directive: C vs. C++ Header Files
summary: Explains the purpose of #include for accessing header files/libraries, and contrasts C-style header filenames (e.g. stdio.h) with the corresponding C++-style header names (e.g. cstdio), presented in a side-by-side comparison table.
main_text: #include Directive. Common usage: To include "header files" that allow us to access functions defined in a separate file or library. For pure C compilers, we include a C header file with its filename: #include <stdlib.h>. For C++ compilers, we include a C header file without the .h extension and prepend a 'c': #include <cstdlib>.
notes_text: The comparison table maps stdio.h/cstdio (I/O and file access: printf, fopen, snprintf) to iostream (cin, cout, cerr); stdlib.h/cstdlib (rand(), memory allocation) to algorithm (find, sort, min/max); string.h/cstring (C-string functions on char arrays) to string (the C++ string class); and math.h/cmath (sin(), pow(), etc.) to vector (an array-like container class), illustrating that C++ often introduces entirely new headers/classes alongside the C-compatible ones.

images.description: A two-column comparison table listing C header files (stdio.h, stdlib.h, string.h, math.h and their C++ 'c'-prefixed equivalents cstdio, cstdlib, cstring, cmath) alongside the C++-only headers iostream, algorithm, string, and vector, each row describing the functionality provided (I/O, memory allocation, C-string functions, math functions, sorting/searching algorithms, the C++ string class, and the vector container class).

title: Common Casting Errors: Casting Is Temporary and Doesn't Work on Strings
summary: Warns that casting only temporarily changes a value's type for one expression (not permanently), and that casting does not work for converting to/from strings -- string library functions like to_string(), stoi(), and stod() must be used instead.
main_text: Common Casting Errors. Only changes the type temporarily for the sake of the expression (not a permanent type change). Casting only really works on numeric types and NOT strings (different than many other languages like Python). When converting to/from a string, do NOT use casting, but functions from the string library (to_string(), stoi(), stod(), etc.).
notes_text: Code examples show: 'int b = static_cast<int>(a) / 2;' works and truncates a temporarily (a itself stays 3.6 afterward); 'string d = static_cast<string>(c);' fails to compile, but 'string d = to_string(c);' works; 'int f = static_cast<int>(e);' (where e is a string "42") fails to compile, but 'int f = stoi(e);' works. The memory diagram contrasts the string "42" (stored as ASCII bytes 52, 50, 00 for '4', '2', '\0') with the actual integer 42 (stored as the 4-byte binary value 00 00 00 42), visually explaining why casting a string to int is nonsensical -- they have completely different byte-level representations.

images.description: A memory-layout comparison showing the C-string "42" stored as three ASCII bytes (52, 50, 00 representing '4', '2', and the null terminator) versus the actual 4-byte integer value 42 (00 00 00 42), connected by a 'not equal' symbol to visually explain why static_cast<int>("42") does not work the way casting a numeric type does -- strings and numbers have fundamentally different binary representations.

title: Statements: Common Kinds of C++ Statements
summary: Categorizes the common kinds of C++ statements that make up functions -- declarations, assignment+expression, assignment+function call, cin/cout statements, and return statements -- each ending in a semicolon.
main_text: Statements. C/C++ functions are composed of statements. Most common kinds of statements end with a semicolon. Declarations (e.g. int x=3;). Assignment + Expression (suppose int x=3; int y;): x = x * 5 / 9; // compute the expression & place result in x; x = (3*5)/9 = 15/9 = 1. Assignment + Function Call (+ Expression): x = cos(0.0) + 1.5; sin(3.14); // Must save or print out the result (x = sin(3.14), etc.). cin, cout statements + Expressions: cout << cos(0.0) + 1.5 << " is the answer." << endl; Return statement (immediately ends a function): return expression; // (more on this later).
notes_text: Notes that a bare function call like 'sin(3.14);' with no assignment or output statement computes a value that is immediately discarded, echoing the earlier 'Common Mistake: Forgetting to Assign' lesson.

title: Exercises: average, rad2deg, and Celsius-to-Fahrenheit Conversion
summary: Lists three hands-on coding exercises for students to complete using an online C++ compiler: 'average', 'rad2deg', and writing a program to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit using the formula F = 9/5*C + 32.
main_text: Exercises. Exercises: average; rad2deg. Write a program to convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit [F = 9/5 * C + 32]. Use http://cpp.sh or http://onlinegdb.com (or EdStem Workspace, if available).
notes_text: Points students to external online C++ compilers (cpp.sh, onlinegdb.com) or the course's EdStem Workspace to complete these hands-on practice exercises applying expressions, casting, and math functions covered earlier in the unit.

title: Section Divider: Assignment and Ordering
summary: Section header slide introducing the topic of how assignment behaves as a copy operation and why statement order/sequence matters.
main_text: ASSIGNMENT AND ORDERING
notes_text: Marks the start of the section covering assignment-as-copy semantics and the classic variable-swap problem.

title: Important: Assignment Means Copy
summary: Explains that assignment makes a copy of a value into the destination variable, leaving the source variable unchanged, and that assignment happens immediately, so the overwritten prior value is lost and statement order matters.
main_text: Important: Assignment Means Copy. Assigning a variable makes a copy. It leaves the source variable unchanged. Is performed immediately and takes effect before the next statement. The overwritten value (5 in this example) can never be recovered. It is lost forever! Order/sequence MATTERS! 1 assignment statement affects subsequent expressions.
notes_text: Example: 'int x = 5, y = 3; x = y; // copy y into x, y still has 3;'. The before/after diagram shows x starting at 5 and y at 3; after 'x = y;', x becomes 3 (a copy of y's value) while y remains 3 unchanged, and the original value 5 that was in x is permanently lost.

images.description: A before/after diagram of two storage bins labeled x and y: before 'x = y;' executes, x holds 5 and y holds 3; after execution, x holds 3 (copied from y) while y remains unchanged at 3, illustrating that the original value 5 in x is permanently overwritten and lost.

title: Challenge: Swap 2 Variables (Naive Attempt)
summary: Poses the classic challenge of swapping the values of two variables, showing a naive but incorrect attempt ('a = b; b = a;') that fails because the first assignment overwrites a's original value before it can be given to b.
main_text: Challenge: Swap 2 Variables. int a = 7, b = 9; // now consider swapping the value of 2 variables; a = b; b = a;
notes_text: The diagram traces the naive attempt: starting with a=7, b=9, after 'a = b;' both a and b become 9 (a's original 7 is lost), and after 'b = a;' b simply stays 9 -- the swap fails because a's original value was overwritten before it could be copied into b. This sets up the correct three-step temp-variable solution on the next slide.

images.description: A sequence of storage-bin diagrams tracing the naive (incorrect) two-line swap attempt: starting with a=7 and b=9, after 'a = b;' both bins show 9 (a's original value 7 is overwritten and lost), and after 'b = a;' b remains 9, demonstrating that this naive approach fails to actually swap the two values.

title: More Assignments: Swapping with a Temporary Variable
summary: Resolves the swap challenge by introducing a third temporary variable to hold one value during the swap, walking through the three-step correct solution, and previews a follow-up '4-variable swap' challenge exercise.
main_text: More Assignments. Assigning a variable makes a copy; it leaves the source variable unchanged. Example: Swap the value of 2 variables. Easiest method: Use a 3rd temporary variable to save one value and then replace that variable. Challenge: 4swap exercise. Code: int a = 7, b = 9, temp; temp = a; a = b; b = temp; cout << a << " " << b << endl;
notes_text: The three numbered steps in the diagram are: 1) temp = a; (temp now holds a's original value 7), 2) a = b; (a becomes 9), 3) b = temp; (b becomes 7, the value saved in temp) -- correctly swapping a and b to a=9, b=7. The 'Challenge: 4swap exercise' hints at extending this technique to swap or rotate values among four variables.

images.description: A three-step storage-bin diagram showing the correct variable-swap technique using a temporary variable: step 1, temp copies a's value (7); step 2, a is overwritten with b's value (9); step 3, b is overwritten with temp's saved value (7), resulting in a=9 and b=7, a successful swap.

title: Section Divider: Solutions

title: When To Introduce a Variable: Solutions
summary: The completed version of the earlier 'When To Introduce a Variable' slide, with the previously blank code examples filled in (declaring 'string username, password;' and 'int currentSum = 0;').
main_text: When To Introduce a Variable (Solutions). When a value will be input (via cin) and/or change at run-time (as the program executes): string username, password; cin >> username >> password; When a value is computed/updated at one time and used (many times) later: int currentSum = 0; To make the code more readable by another human: double a = (x+34) * (n*6.25); // readability of above vs. below; double height = x + 34; double width = n * 6.25; double area = height * width;

title: Exercise: Trace the Code - Solutions
summary: The completed version of the earlier code-tracing exercise, showing the traced values of 'value' and 'amount' at each step, with final printed outputs of -12, 9.4, and 1.
main_text: Exercise: Trace the Code Below (Solutions). Program: int value = 1; value = (value + 5) * (value - 3); cout << value << endl; double amount = 2.5; value = 7; amount = value + 6 / amount; cout << amount << endl; cout << value % 3 << endl. Traced values -- value: 1, then -12, then 7; amount: 2.5, then 9.4. Printed outputs: -12, 9.4, 1.
notes_text: Trace explanation: 'value = (1+5)*(1-3) = 6*(-2) = -12' (first cout prints -12). Then 'value = 7;' and 'amount = 7 + 6/2.5 = 7 + 2.4 = 9.4' (second cout prints 9.4, using double division since amount is a double). Finally 'value % 3' = '7 % 3' = 1 (third cout prints 1).

title: Exercises: Predict the Output - Solutions
summary: The completed version of the earlier 'predict the output' exercises, revealing that the first program prints 13 then 5, and the second program (dozens/gpa) prints '3 dozen is 36 items.' then 'Your gpa is 3.8333'.
main_text: Exercises (Solutions). Program 1 (int x=5, y=3; double z = x % y * 6 + x / y; ... ) prints: 13 // or 13.0, then 5 // or 5.0. Program 2 (dozens/gpa program) prints: 3 dozen is 36 items., then Your gpa is 3.8333.
notes_text: Program 1 trace: x % y = 5%3 = 2; 2*6 = 12; x/y = 5/3 = 1 (integer division); 12+1 = 13, stored into double z, printed as 13. Then z = 1.0/4*(13-5)+3 = 0.25*8+3 = 2+3 = 5, printed as 5. Program 2 trace: num = 12*3 = 36; gpa = (2*4.0)+(4*3.7) = 8+14.8 = 22.8; gpa /= 6 -> 22.8/6 = 3.8 (double division since gpa is a double), displayed with extra precision as 3.8333.
